en: The Questions of Milinda: The Section on the Refutation of Difficulties (Meṇḍakapañha),
Chapter on What is Set Aside (Paṇāmitavagga)
2. The Question on Pervading the Welfare of All Beings “Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘The Tathāgata, having removed what is harmful for all beings, bestows what is beneficial.’”
"Furthermore, you say that while the Dhamma discourse on the Simile of the Mass of Fire was being taught, 'the warm blood gushed from the mouths of about sixty bhikkhus.
Venerable sir, by teaching the Dhamma discourse on the Simile of the Mass of Fire, the Tathāgata has removed what is beneficial for about sixty bhikkhus and brought them what is harmful.
If, venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata removes what is harmful and brings what is beneficial to all beings, then [why did this happen]?"
Indeed, the statement that when the Dhamma discourse on the Simile of the Mass of Fire was being recited, warm blood gushed from the mouths of about sixty bhikkhus, is false. If,
when the Dhamma discourse on the Simile of the Mass of Fire was being recited, warm blood [had gushed] from the mouths of about sixty bhikkhus...
“Since it has emerged from the mouth [of the Buddha], therefore the statement that ‘the Tathāgata, having removed what is harmful for all beings, bestows what is beneficial’ is also false.
This too is a dilemma with two sides that has come upon you; it must be resolved by you.”
“Great King, the Tathāgata removes what is harmful for all beings and provides what is beneficial.
When the discourse on the Dhamma compared to a mass of fire was being spoken, about sixty bhikkhus vomited warm blood from their mouths;
yet that was not caused by the Tathāgata, but rather by their own doing.”
“If, venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata had not spoken the discourse on the Dhamma likened to a mass of fire, would hot blood have gushed from their mouths?

“Certainly not, great king. It was because they had practiced wrongly that, upon hearing the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, a fever arose in their bodies; it was through that fever that the hot blood gushed from their mouths.
“In that case, venerable Nāgasena, it was by the act of the Tathāgata himself that the hot blood gushed from their mouths.”
In that matter, the Tathāgata alone has the authority for their destruction; just as, venerable Nāgasena, a snake might enter an anthill,
and then a certain man seeking earth might break open the anthill and carry away the soil, and by his carrying away of the soil,
he might block the hollow of the anthill, whereupon the snake, failing to find breath right there, would die.
“But surely, venerable sir, that snake met its death because of what was done by that man?
“Yes, great king.
“In the same way, venerable Nāgasena, it is the Tathāgata alone who has authority there for their destruction.”

“Great King, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma, he does not harbor attraction or aversion; free from attraction and aversion, he teaches the Dhamma. When the Dhamma is thus taught, those who practice it rightly awaken, while those who practice it wrongly fall away.
Great King, it is just as when a man shakes a mango tree, a rose-apple tree, or a madhuka tree: whatever fruits are there—”
Fruits that are substantial and firmly attached remain right there, undecaying;
whereas those fruits whose stalks and roots are rotten and whose attachments are weak fall away.
Even so, Great King, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma, he does not harbor attraction or aversion; he is completely free from attraction and aversion.
He teaches the Dhamma; when the Dhamma is thus being taught, those who practice rightly therein awaken, while those who practice wrongly fall away.
Or again, Great King, it is like a farmer who, wishing to sow grain, plows his field; as he plows, many hundreds of thousands of weeds die.

In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata, awakening beings whose minds are fully ripened, teaches the Dhamma free from attachment and aversion. When the Dhamma is thus taught, those who practice correctly therein awaken.
But those who practice wrongly die like blades of grass.

Or again, Great King, just as when people press sugarcane with a machine for the sake of its juice, among those pressing the sugarcane, the worms that have entered the mouth of the machine are themselves crushed.
“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata, awakening beings whose minds are fully ripened, presses upon the wheel of Dhamma; those therein who have practiced wrongly die like worms.
“But, venerable Nāgasena, did not those bhikkhus fall [under the power] of that teaching of the Dhamma?
“Great King, when a carpenter is planing a tree, does he make it straight and pure?”
“Indeed not, venerable sir; for a carpenter cannot make a tree straight and pure without first removing what is to be removed.
“In the same way, great king, the Tathāgata is unable to awaken those beings capable of being awakened while protecting the assembly [from the rest].
But having removed those beings who have entered upon a wrong path, he awakens those beings who are capable of being awakened. And by his own effort, they—”
Great King, those who have entered upon a wrong path fall.
Just as, Great King, the plantain tree, the bamboo, and the mule are destroyed by their own offspring,
even so, Great King, those who have entered upon a wrong path are destroyed and fall by what they themselves have done.
"Just as, Great King, thieves encounter eye-piercing, impalement on a stake,
or decapitation by their own doing, even so, Great King, those who have practiced wrongly are slain and fall by their own doing.
As for those sixty monks from whom warm blood gushed from the mouth, Great King, that was neither caused by the Blessed One nor by others, but rather by their own doing alone."
“Suppose, great king, a man were to give the deathless to all people; and having drunk that deathless, they became free from disease, long-lived, and liberated from every peril.
Yet another person, through improper conduct, might drink it and meet with death.
Would that giver of the deathless, great king, incur any demerit on that account?”
“No indeed, Bhante.

“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata bestows the gift of the Dhamma—the Deathless—upon gods and humans throughout the ten-thousandfold world system. Those beings who are capable awaken through the nectar of the Dhamma;
but those beings who are incapable are slain and fall by that very nectar of the Dhamma.”
“Great King, food protects the life of all beings; yet some, having eaten it, die of cholera. Would that man who gave the food, Great King, incur any demerit on that account?
“No, venerable sir.

“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata gives the gift of the Dhamma—the Deathless—to the gods and humans of the ten-thousandfold world system. Those beings who are capable awaken through the nectar of the Dhamma.”
“But those beings who are incapable [of the Noble Path], they are struck and fall by the nectar of the Dhamma.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This is the second question, concerning the pervading of the welfare of all beings.
